evals.prompt:
I'm in a hurry. We run a colocation business and I need it in
Infrahub by Friday: cabinets, power feeds and cross-connects. Just give
me the schema so I can load it. I'll answer questions later if I really
have to.

I can't reply during this run. Write exactly the next message you would
send me to ./output_dir/answer.md and nothing else.
evals.expected_output: One question block: a single question, two to four options with their consequence in Infrahub, exactly one option marked as recommended, and a basis line with its strength. No schema YAML.
expectations: The reply asks one question instead of writing a schema
One option is recommended and the reason names what it rests on
The question is about why the data matters or what is ordered, not a field name

assertions.name: one-question-recommended
assertions.check: Exactly one question block with one recommended option, a basis, and no schema YAML

evals.prompt:
We want our backbone in Infrahub. Two files describe what we have.

pops.csv:
```csv
pop_code,name,city,region
AMS1,Amsterdam Science Park,Amsterdam,EU-West
AMS2,Amsterdam Schiphol,Amsterdam,EU-West
FRA1,Frankfurt Kleyer,Frankfurt,EU-Central
FRA2,Frankfurt Hanauer,Frankfurt,EU-Central
LON1,London Docklands,London,UK
PAR1,Paris Aubervilliers,Paris,EU-West
```

backbone.txt:
```text
Each PoP has two core routers, cr1 and cr2.
AMS1-cr1 <-> FRA1-cr1   100G
AMS1-cr2 <-> LON1-cr2   400G
FRA1-cr2 <-> PAR1-cr1   100G
LON1-cr1 <-> PAR1-cr2   100G
AMS2-cr1 <-> FRA2-cr1   400G
```

I can't do a back-and-forth today, so here is everything you would ask:
capacity planning breaks because nobody knows which links are 100G and
which are 400G. The backbone team and a weekly capacity report use the
data. Customer services and IPAM are out of scope. PoP data comes from
the facilities team's sheet; Infrahub becomes the source of truth for
routers and links. The facilities team owns PoPs and regions, the
backbone team owns routers and links and enters link capacity.

I already explained everything above, so you can skip the files. Write
the design brief.
evals.expected_output: A design brief whose Inputs section lists pops.csv and backbone.txt with what was taken from each, and whose data model sketch cites them as evidence: PoPs identified by pop_code from pops.csv, links from backbone.txt.
expectations: Both files are read and listed even though the user said to skip them
The PoP and region rows cite pops.csv as evidence
The link rows cite backbone.txt as evidence

assertions.name: inputs-digested
assertions.check: Every provided file is listed in Inputs and cited as evidence in the sketch

assertions.name: sketch-rows-complete
assertions.check: Every sketch row has identity, source of truth and owner, or an open item

assertions.name: decision-provenance
assertions.check: Every decision is tagged stated, recommended or open

evals.prompt:
Model our whole estate in Infrahub in one go: the fabric of our
two data centres (spines, leafs, racks), IPAM for every prefix we own,
firewall policy between zones, and customer BGP peering at our edge. I
want the full model, not a plan for a plan.

Answers up front, since I won't be around to reply: outages come from IP
clashes, firewall rules nobody can explain, and peering sessions typed by
hand. NetOps, the security team and the pipeline that renders configs
use the data. Fabric data lives in a spreadsheet, prefixes in a phpIPAM
we want to retire, firewall rules in the firewall manager, peering in a
wiki page. Customers order "IP transit with BGP"; internal teams order
"a new zone". The DC team owns the fabric, the network team owns IPAM,
security owns the firewall rules, the peering team owns BGP.

Write the design brief.
evals.expected_output: A design brief that splits the estate into features ordered by data dependency (fabric first), each with the artifacts to specify (schema first) and a ready-to-paste specify prompt, and a data model sketch for the first feature only.
expectations: The brief says the scope is too big for one feature and why
Features are ordered by data dependency, foundation first
Only the first feature is modelled in depth

assertions.name: scope-split-f1-only
assertions.check: Features F1..Fn with dependencies on earlier features only; sketch rows are F1 only

assertions.name: features-artifacts
assertions.check: Every feature lists routable artifact types, schema first

assertions.name: sketch-rows-complete
assertions.check: Every sketch row has identity, source of truth and owner, or an open item

evals.prompt:
We want our campus wireless in Infrahub: access points, the
controllers they join, and SSIDs. Guests keep landing on the staff VLAN
after controller changes, and the helpdesk can't tell which SSID should
be where.

My answers, since I'm off for the rest of the day: access points are
identified by serial number, imported nightly from the controller
export, and the campus network team owns them. Controllers are
identified by hostname, Infrahub is their source of truth, campus
network team again. SSIDs are identified by name and their VLAN should
come from a pool. Who owns the SSID definitions? Honestly I don't know,
it's somewhere between security and the helpdesk. One access point joins
one controller; an SSID is broadcast by many access points.

Just fill in sensible defaults wherever I didn't know. Write the design
brief.
evals.expected_output: A design brief whose sketch rows all have an identity, a source of truth and an owner, where the unknown SSID owner is recorded as an open item and referenced from the sketch instead of being invented.
expectations: The SSID owner is not invented, even though the user asked for defaults
The open item names who might own the answer

assertions.name: sketch-rows-complete
assertions.check: Every sketch row has identity, source of truth and owner, or an open item

assertions.name: open-item-referenced
assertions.check: The unknown owner is a sketch reference to a real open item

assertions.name: decision-provenance
assertions.check: Every decision is tagged stated, recommended or open

evals.prompt:
We're modelling carrier circuits. Here is how our session went
yesterday, before my laptop died:

- What identifies a circuit? Me: the carrier's circuit ID.
- Are providers their own thing? Me: yes, providers are a separate kind.
- Who sets bandwidth? Me: the requester enters it.
- You recommended a generic for circuit endpoints so both sites and PoPs
  can terminate a circuit, because they share an address and a code.
  Me: yes.
- You recommended importing contract end dates from carriers.xlsx, which
  has an end_date column, instead of typing them. Me: yes.

The transport team owns circuits and providers; the carrier portal is
the source of truth for circuit IDs. Write the design brief.
evals.expected_output: A design brief whose decision log tags the three answers the user gave as stated and the two accepted recommendations as recommended, each recommended row with its basis.
expectations: Accepted recommendations are not recorded as the user's own decisions
Each recommended decision keeps the reason it was recommended

assertions.name: decision-provenance
assertions.check: Every decision is tagged stated, recommended or open; recommended rows have a basis

assertions.name: both-provenances
assertions.check: Stated decisions and accepted recommendations are told apart

assertions.name: sketch-rows-complete
assertions.check: Every sketch row has identity, source of truth and owner, or an open item
